  age: 59

  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced

  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Vignette:
Marisol Fuentes is a 59-year-old divorced Latina woman who works as a licensed physical therapist at an outpatient rehabilitation clinic in a mid-sized city in Texas. She came to therapy carrying what she described as a tiredness she could no longer explain away — a weight that had been building quietly for decades and had finally, in recent months, become impossible to set down.

Marisol grew up in a household where her primary caregiver — her maternal uncle, who assumed guardianship after her mother's illness — was unpredictably and sometimes severely physically abusive. The violence did not follow a pattern she could ever reliably anticipate. It could erupt in the kitchen while she was doing homework, or in the hallway when she came home from school. What she remembered most vividly, when she allowed herself to remember it at all, was the particular quality of not knowing where he was in the house — listening for footsteps, positioning herself near doorways, keeping the wall at her back whenever she sat at the table so that no one could come up behind her. She learned early that visibility meant survival: if she could see the room, she could read it.

For much of her adult life, Marisol managed to keep those years at a careful distance. She built a career that gave her structure and purpose. She raised two children largely on her own after her marriage ended in her thirties. She was known at the clinic as exceptionally competent and quietly self-contained. But in the past year, following the death of a close colleague and a subsequent restructuring at work that required her to take on a larger caseload with unfamiliar staff, something began to shift.

Fragments of memory started surfacing without invitation — a flash of a particular hallway, the sound of a belt, the specific texture of linoleum under her palms — and then vanishing before she could hold them. When she tried to sit with what had happened to her as a child, she found herself able to narrate events in a flat, almost clinical voice, as though recounting something that had befallen someone else entirely. The story felt so extreme, so outside the bounds of what she believed her life had actually contained, that she sometimes doubted her own history. It was hard to believe it actually happened to me, she told her therapist in their second session. She did not say this with distress. She said it with the same careful neutrality she might use to describe a patient's imaging results.

At the clinic, the hypervigilance that had once been invisible to her had become harder to ignore. She consistently manoeuvred to take the chair with her back against the wall in team meetings. When a new patient — a large man — entered her treatment room unexpectedly while she was charting, she felt a surge of alarm so acute that she had to excuse herself to the corridor. She had come to believe, without quite articulating it, that strangers approaching her in ordinary situations represented a genuine and immediate threat. The belief was not rational to her in daylight; it was simply true in her body.

At night, she woke repeatedly to check the apartment — the locks, the windows, the rooms. She ate heavily in the evenings, working through the contents of her refrigerator in a way that she recognised as purposeful distraction rather than hunger. On weekends, she cleaned and reorganised her apartment with a thoroughness that felt necessary rather than optional, rearranging cupboards and linen closets until something internal quieted, at least briefly. She had stopped attending her book club, declined invitations from her daughters, and quietly arranged her life to minimise anything that might introduce unpredictability or demand.

What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her younger daughter, who told her gently but directly that she seemed to be disappearing. Marisol sat with that for several weeks before making the call. What she most feared, she said at intake, was that opening any of this would make it more real than she could manage. What she most hoped for, she admitted more quietly, was to stop waking up afraid in a home she had spent thirty years making safe.
